title: MongoDB: Modeling, Indexing & Scaling
primer: MongoDB performance is query-driven: indexes follow real filters and sort keys, not the ER diagram. Embedding wins for co-accessed bounded data; references win when data is shared, large, or unbounded. At scale, shard key cardinality and hotspot avoidance matter more than 'just add shards,' and scatter-gather queries punish bad access patterns.

cheatStrip.v: Embed bounded co-read data; ref shared/unbounded
Cap size; bucket or child collection if unbounded
Query lacks shard key → fans out to all shards
Batched bulkWrite with resume token / _id cursor

quiz.q: What makes an unbounded array dangerous in a document?

options.t: Document growth, expensive updates, and 16MB limit risk

quiz.explain: Growing arrays bloat documents, slow updates/rewrites, and can hit the 16MB BSON limit.

quiz.q: A query without the shard key in a sharded cluster typically:

options.t: Automatically routes to one shard via _id

quiz.explain: Without shard-key equality (or a selective prefix), mongos must query many/all shards.

quiz.q: Best first step for a slow frequent query on 100M docs?

options.t: explain() and confirm index use / docs examined
Switch the entire app to aggregation

quiz.explain: Prove COLLSCAN vs IXSCAN and examine ratio before bigger changes.

options.t: tenantId on every query and compound indexes starting with it
A separate MongoDB process per HTTP request

quiz.explain: Defense in depth: query predicates, indexes, and preferably enforced filters in the data access layer.

questions.question: A MongoDB collection has 100 million documents and a frequently used query became slow. What would you inspect first?
questions.first30s: I would capture the exact filter/sort/projection, run explain('executionStats'), and check whether we still hit an index or started scanning millions of docs.
modelAnswer: Confirm the query shape from production logs (filter, sort, collation, hint) — small predicate changes kill index use.
Run explain('executionStats'): winning plan, IXSCAN vs COLLSCAN, keysExamined / docsExamined / nReturned ratio.
Check index list and usage (existing indexes, partial/sparse, ESR rule: Equality, Sort, Range).
Look at working set vs RAM, replication lag, and whether the collection recently grew past cache.
Fix with a compound index matching the query, covered projection if possible, then re-measure; only then consider schema or shard changes.
questions.sayIt: First explain executionStats. If docsExamined ≫ nReturned, the index or query shape is wrong — I fix that before talking about sharding.
questions.nestNote: Log slow queries with filter keys (not necessarily full PII values) from the Mongo driver.
traps: Adding indexes blindly without explain
Sorting in memory because the index doesn't include the sort key
Blaming 'Mongo is slow' when the query is a collection scan
followUps: What is a covered query?

questions.question: How would you decide between embedding and referencing for a MongoDB document model?
questions.first30s: Embed when data is read together, has clear ownership, and stays bounded. Reference when shared, independently updated, or unbounded.
modelAnswer: Ask access patterns: one read should ideally get what the API needs — embed those fields.
Embed: address on order, small config blobs, bounded comment previews — atomic updates with the parent.
Reference: users shared across docs, large media metadata, infinite event histories.
Hybrid: embed a denormalized snapshot (product name at order time) and keep a reference for the source of truth.
Revisit when document size, update contention, or fan-out updates become painful.
questions.sayIt: Modeling follows queries. Embed co-read bounded data; reference shared or unbounded data — and denormalize snapshots when history must not change.
questions.nestNote: Avoid generic repository patterns that force relational joins via $lookup everywhere.
traps: Embedding unbounded arrays 'for convenience'
Referencing everything and $lookup-joining like SQL by default
Forgetting denormalized snapshots go stale on purpose (or not)
followUps: When is $lookup acceptable in hot paths?
How do you update denormalized fields across many documents?

questions.question: An aggregation pipeline is slow in production. How would you identify the expensive stage and optimize it?
questions.first30s: I explain the aggregation, find the stage with the biggest time/docs, and push $match/$sort early with indexes — avoid blowing up with $lookup or unbounded $group.
modelAnswer: Run aggregate([...], { explain: true }) / explain('executionStats') and identify costly stages.
Move selective $match (and $sort+$limit) as early as possible so later stages see fewer docs; ensure indexes support that match/sort.
Watch $lookup (N+1 style blowups), $unwind on large arrays, and $group spilling to disk.
Project only needed fields early; avoid returning huge intermediate documents.
Consider pre-aggregations, materialized collections, or changing the schema if the pipeline is a permanent hot path.
questions.sayIt: Find the expensive stage, filter early with an index, and treat $lookup/$unwind/$group as suspects until proven cheap.
questions.nestNote: Prefer indexed finds for simple queries; aggregation is for multi-stage transforms.
traps: $match after $lookup on the full collection
Using aggregation when a compound index + find would suffice
Ignoring allowDiskUse as a permanent crutch
followUps: How do you index for $match + $sort + $limit?
When would you use a materialized view collection?

questions.question: How would you choose MongoDB indexes from real query patterns rather than from the schema alone?
questions.first30s: I inventory the top queries by frequency and latency, then design compound indexes for those predicates — schema fields alone don't tell me selectivity or sort order.
modelAnswer: Collect slow/query logs or APM: filter keys, sort, projection, frequency.
Apply ESR: Equality fields first, then Sort, then Range — build compound indexes accordingly.
Prefer one compound index that serves a critical query over many single-field indexes.
Use partial indexes for hot subsets (e.g. status: 'open') and TTL indexes for expiring data.
Drop unused indexes after verifying; every index costs write amplification and RAM.
questions.sayIt: Indexes follow the workload. I rank real queries, build compound keys with ESR, and delete indexes that only look good on the schema.
questions.code:
// Query: { tenantId, status } sort createdAt
db.orders.createIndex({ tenantId: 1, status: 1, createdAt: -1 })
questions.nestNote: Review indexes in PR checklist whenever a new repository query is added.
traps: Indexing every field 'just in case'
Left-prefix mistakes (index unused because equality order wrong)
Ignoring collation / case-insensitive needs
followUps: How do multikey indexes on arrays behave?
What's the cost of too many indexes on a write-heavy collection?

questions.question: A document contains an array that grows indefinitely and is frequently queried. How would you redesign the model?
questions.first30s: Unbounded arrays are a modeling smell — I'd move events into a child collection keyed by parent id, or bucket by time, and keep only a bounded recent slice embedded if needed.
modelAnswer: Diagnose: document size growth, slow $push/$pull, multikey index bloat, risk of 16MB limit.
Extract the array into a separate collection: { parentId, …, createdAt } with indexes on parentId + createdAt.
Optionally keep a bounded embedded preview (last N) for fast reads of the parent.
For high-volume time series, use bucketing (one doc per day/hour) instead of one mega-array.
Migrate with batched reads/writes; update queries to page the child collection.
questions.sayIt: Infinite arrays don't belong in one document. Child collection or time buckets, maybe a small embedded preview for the hot read.
questions.nestNote: API pagination should target the events collection, not load the whole parent.
traps: Capping with $slice in queries but still storing unbounded data
Using $unwind on huge arrays in hot aggregations
One document per user that accumulates lifetime history
followUps: How do you migrate without dual-write races?
When are bucket patterns better than one-doc-per-event?

questions.question: How would you choose a shard key for a high-write MongoDB workload?
questions.first30s: I need high cardinality and even write distribution so inserts don't hammer one chunk/shard, while still supporting targeted queries with that key.
modelAnswer: List write pattern and top queries that must be targeted (avoid scatter-gather on hot paths).
Prefer a key with high cardinality and monotonic-write awareness — pure increasing _id/timestamps can hotspot on one shard.
Common pattern: { tenantId, _id } or hashed field when range queries aren't needed; compound keys for tenant isolation + uniqueness.
Avoid low-cardinality keys (status, country) that create jumbo hot chunks.
Load-test distribution; plan for resharding cost if the key is wrong — choosing carefully beats early sharding.
questions.sayIt: Shard key = cardinality + even writes + targeted reads. I won't shard on status or plain timestamps that create hot shards.
questions.code:
// Example: tenant-scoped compound shard key
sh.shardCollection('app.orders', { tenantId: 1, _id: 1 })
questions.nestNote: Include shard key fields in repository query helpers so developers can't omit them easily.
traps: Sharding on low-cardinality fields
Assuming more shards fix a hotspot key
Picking a key that forces scatter-gather on every API read
followUps: Hashed vs ranged shard keys — trade-offs?
What is a jumbo chunk?

questions.question: What characteristics can make a MongoDB shard key a hotspot?
questions.first30s: Low cardinality, monotonically increasing values, or a popular tenant/key that attracts most writes — all funnel inserts to one chunk or shard.
modelAnswer: Monotonic keys (Date, ObjectId time portion, auto-inc) send new writes to the highest chunk — right-hand hotspot.
Low cardinality (enum status, boolean) creates few fat chunks that can't split usefully.
Skewed real-world distribution: one celebrity tenantId dominates traffic.
Hot documents updated constantly on one shard key value.
Mitigations: hashed keys, compound keys with high-cardinality suffix, isolate whales, or rethink access patterns.
questions.sayIt: Hotspots come from monotonic inserts, low cardinality, or traffic skew. The key must spread writes, not just unique them.
traps: Thinking 'unique' equals 'well distributed'
Hashing away range queries you still need without a plan
Ignoring one mega-tenant after choosing tenantId alone
followUps: How do you detect imbalance across shards in metrics?
Can you change a shard key later and what does it cost?

questions.question: A query becomes scatter/gather in a sharded cluster. What does that mean for performance and how would you reduce it?
questions.first30s: Scatter-gather means mongos fans the query to many/all shards and merges results — latency and load scale with shard count. I reduce it by including the shard key in queries or redesigning the key/access path.
modelAnswer: Confirm in explain: shards touched, sorting/merging on mongos, high cumulative docs examined.
Add shard-key equality (or selective prefix) to hot queries so they become targeted.
For pagination/sort without shard key, expect merge cost — prefer targeted queries or precomputed views.
If the business query can never include the shard key, reconsider shard key or duplicate data into a query-optimized collection.
Monitor mongos CPU and per-shard ops; scatter-gather under load becomes a cluster-wide amplification bug.
questions.sayIt: Scatter-gather fans out to every shard. Hot paths must be targeted by shard key — otherwise each read taxes the whole cluster.
questions.nestNote: Lint or wrapper: require tenantId in find criteria for sharded tenant collections.
traps: Assuming secondary indexes make queries targeted (they don't replace shard key routing)
Adding shards to 'fix' scatter-gather (often makes it worse)
Sorting globally without limits on scatter queries
followUps: How does mongos merge sorted results?
When is scatter-gather acceptable?

questions.question: You need to update tens of millions of MongoDB documents. How would you make the migration safe, resumable, and observable?
questions.first30s: Batched bulkWrite by _id ranges with a checkpoint, idempotent updates, rate limits, and metrics — never one multi-update that can't resume.
modelAnswer: Design idempotent document transforms (safe to re-run) and a migration version field if needed.
Iterate with a cursor/_id range; bulkWrite ordered:false in batches (e.g. 500–1000); persist lastProcessedId checkpoint.
Throttle (sleep/token bucket) to protect WT cache and replication lag; pause when lag or CPU exceeds SLO.
Observe: documents/sec, errors, lag, percent complete; dead-letter failed _ids.
Verify with sampling/checksums; support resume after crash from checkpoint.
questions.sayIt: Big migrations are checkpointed bulkWrite loops — idempotent, throttled, observable, and resumable from last _id.
questions.nestNote: Run as a worker job with lock so two migrators don't double-load the cluster.
traps: updateMany on the whole collection with no resume story
Unordered bulk without tracking per-doc failures
Migrating at full speed until secondary lag pages someone
followUps: How do you dual-write during expand-contract in Mongo?
When would you use change streams for migration?

questions.question: How would you design multi-tenant data isolation in MongoDB?
questions.first30s: Choose isolation tier: shared collection with tenantId, database-per-tenant, or cluster-per-tenant for the noisiest/compliance-heavy customers — enforce tenant predicates in every query.
modelAnswer: Default: shared collection(s) with tenantId on every document; compound indexes starting with tenantId; shard key often includes tenantId.
Enforce isolation in the data access layer (mandatory filter), not only in controllers; consider atlas/server-side validation or wrappers.
Stronger isolation: separate database per tenant for compliance/noisy neighbors; highest: dedicated cluster.
Never trust client-supplied tenantId alone — bind from authenticated session.
Test for cross-tenant leakage; audit queries missing tenantId; watch jumbo tenants for hotspot/shard skew.
questions.sayIt: tenantId on every doc and every query, indexes and shard key aligned, auth-bound tenant — escalate to DB- or cluster-per-tenant when compliance or noise demands it.
questions.code:
db.orders.createIndex({ tenantId: 1, createdAt: -1 })
db.orders.find({ tenantId: auth.tenantId, … })
questions.nestNote: Nest middleware/CLS can inject tenantId into repositories so handlers can't omit it.
traps: Filtering tenant only in the UI
Unique indexes that aren't tenant-scoped (email global vs per-tenant)
One mega-tenant melting a shared shard
followUps: How do unique constraints work per tenant?
When do you move a tenant to its own database?
